input.evidence_text: Doorman who witnessed racist outburst says abuse 'becoming normal' - BBC News Image caption, Jawad Ali, 20, said he now expects racial abuse when he goes to work By Kaya Black North West Published 1 hour ago A doorman who shared a video of a racist outburst he witnessed while at work has said such abuse towards staff is becoming "normalised". The footage, taken outside Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale, Greater Manchester, showed a woman shouting abuse and making gestures at a black security guard. Jawad Ali said the club-goer became abusive after being asked to move away from an exit while he was working at the venue on Saturday night. Greater Manchester Police said it had received a report about the incident and inquiries were ongoing. Image caption, Footage of the incident has been shared widely online "It's disgusting," said Jawad, 20, who was working for Protective One Security at the time. "This isn't the first time, and it won't be the last," he added. Jawad said during the past two years working on the doors he has been called every racial slur and even threatened with death. "I expect now when I come to work to be racially abused one night out of the four that I work," he continued. "Its a normal thing now. It should be a big thing that gets prosecuted heavily." Image caption, The incident happened outside Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale Fellow security worker Liz Turley, who works for Radius Security, said: "There hasn't been a night where I haven't experienced some instance of somebody standing there for a prolonged period of time giving me abuse." title: Social media a factor in HMO attacks, says police boss

input.lead: Greater Manchester Police said 46 properties were damaged across Greater Manchester since 5 October
input.summary: Greater Manchester Police said 46 properties were damaged across Greater Manchester since 5 October
input.evidence_text: Social media a factor in HMO attacks, says police boss - BBC News Image source, LDRS/MEN Image caption, Police said there had been 46 properties damaged across the city region since 5 October By Naj Modak , North West and Ed Barnes , Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 1 hour ago Social media is in part behind a spate of recent "racially or religiously motivated" attacks on houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) across Greater Manchester, a senior police officer has said. Greater Manchester Police said there had been 46 properties damaged across the city region since 5 October, including in Salford, Tameside and Stockport. Ch Sup Marcus Noden said footage of criminal damage was being shared widely "followed by comments and discussions", and people were using social media to "push the message out across different areas". He warned people to stop the attacks, which he said were "unlawful, reckless and putting lives at risk". As an investigation into the run of criminal damage continues, a 33-year-old man was arrested on Wednesday morning on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage and remained in custody for questioning. The damage was to HMOs or properties that were mistaken for HMOs. In Salford, 41 properties were targeted with three in Tameside and two in Stockport over the period. Image source, LDRS/MEN Image caption, Windows are seen boarded up on one property due to concerns of further attacks According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , last week, two properties in Heaton Norris just outside Stockport town centre were targeted with anti-HMO graffiti. title: More than 100 hopefuls flock to Manchester cafe to apply for job

input.lead: The manager of the cafe says it "shows how the job market is at the minute"
input.summary: The manager of the cafe says it "shows how the job market is at the minute"
input.evidence_text: More than 100 hopefuls descended on a Manchester cafe to apply for a part-time barista role in what the manager described as "whirlwind" of interest Applicants were invited to attend the Fig & Sparrow in the city's Northern Quarter to present their CVs in person rather than simply apply by email General manager Luke Taylor, 32, said he wanted to meet people face-to-face and added: "It shows how the job market is at the minute "People are turning up on a random Tuesday in a cafe that they have probably never been to, hoping for the best." It follows a recent warning from Prime Minister Andy Burnham that the UK faces an "economic catastrophe" due to the nearly one million young people remaining without work, education or training This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people more opportunities

title: Inquest hears of 'great danger' tip-off before fire murders

input.lead: Social workers were told children were in "great danger" days before a fatal fire, an inquest hears
input.summary: Social workers were told children were in "great danger" days before a fatal fire, an inquest hears
input.evidence_text: Social workers received an anonymous tip-off that children were in "great danger" days before they were murdered in an arson attack, an inquest heard Demi Pearson, 14, her brother, Brandon, eight, and sisters, Lacie, seven, and Lia, three, died after petrol bombs were thrown into their home on Jackson Street, Walkden, Salford, in the early hours of December 11, 2017 Their mother Michelle Pearson, 37, died almost two years later after suffering severe burns A joint inquest into their deaths, now in its third week, is being heard at Bolton Coroners' Court and on Wednesday it heard of social services involvement with the family The hearing was told on 29 November, 2017, less than two weeks before the fatal attack, the social services department at Salford City Council received an anonymous call The caller said: "The children are in a really unsafe environment and in great danger."

title: Sinkhole revealed 50 metre deep mine shaft uneder road

input.lead: Part of Alan Turing Way has been closed since March and is expected to stay shut until mid-December
input.summary: Part of Alan Turing Way has been closed since March and is expected to stay shut until mid-December
input.evidence_text: Sinkhole revealed 50 metre deep mine shaft uneder road - BBC News Image caption, A sinkhole found in March revealed a 50m deep sinkhole By Kevin Fitzpatrick and Rebecca Brahde , North West Published 21 October 2026 Work is taking place to repair a sinkhole which revealed a 50m (164ft) mine shaft under a busy road in east Manchester. Part of the northbound carriageway on Alan Turing Way has been closed since March, when the road surface began to sink. Since then, Manchester City Council has filled the hole with more than 100 tonnes of concrete. It said it expected the route to be open again December. Image caption, Councillor Mandie Shilton Godwin says it has been a "massive job" Mandie Shilton Godwin, the executive member for transport, said it had been a "massive job", adding it had "taken an awfully long time”. She added: "It started in March when the depression was noticed, but it wasn't until the end of September when the team were absolutely sure what the problem was. "Once they were sure what the problem was, then they could begin to put it right. "No one could have anticipated the scale of the void that we found but, once it became apparent, all of our effort went into making sure the site was safe and the road could be reopened." A concrete cap is currently being put over the mine shaft. Work will then need to take place to fill the remaining void beneath the road, and lay a new surface. title: Three more arrests in Alisha Samuels murder investigation

input.lead: Alisha Samuels, 26, was found dead after a disturbance in the Newton Heath area of Manchester
input.summary: Alisha Samuels, 26, was found dead after a disturbance in the Newton Heath area of Manchester
input.evidence_text: Three more arrests in Alisha Samuels murder investigation - BBC News Image source, Family photo Image caption, Alisha Samuels was found dead following a disturbance in the Newton Heath area By Rebecca Brahde North West Published 21 October 2026 Three more arrests have been made in connection with the suspected murder of a woman who was stabbed in a street in Manchester. Alisha Samuels, 26, was found dead after officers were called to a disturbance on Dorking Avenue in the Newton Heath area of the city at about 02:00 BST on Thursday. On Tuesday, Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Dorking Avenue, was charged with the murder of Samuels and the attempted murder of a man. Earlier two men, both 19, were arrested on suspicion of murder and a 48-year-old woman was held on suspicion of assisting an offender, Greater Manchester Police said. Det Ch Insp Justin Bryant said: "We remain focused on establishing the full circumstances and want to reassure Alisha's loved ones that we are committed to securing justice for her. "My thoughts remain with Alisha's family and friends as they continue to come to terms with this devastating loss." The detective renewed an appeal for witnesses or anyone with information to come forward. title: Young adults in North of England face 42% higher death rates

input.lead: The gap between North and South has more than tripled since 1981, despite falling death rates
input.summary: The gap between North and South has more than tripled since 1981, despite falling death rates
input.evidence_text: North West health correspondent Published 21 October 2026 Younger adults living in the North of England are 42% more likely to die than their counterparts in the South, according to new research A study by academics in Manchester and Liverpool found people in the North aged 25 to 49 faced a significantly higher risk of death than people of the same age living in the South Researchers said deprivation was a major factor behind the gap and called for urgent action to tackle inequalities The Department of Health and Social Care (DoHSC) said it was determined to reduce health inequalities and close the divide The research, by the University of Manchester, the University of Liverpool and Health Equity North and published in The Lancet medical journal , external , analysed deaths between 1981 and 2024 in two geographical areas of England, splitting England's population into "two roughly The North encompassed Greater Manchester, Cheshire, Lancashire, Yorkshire, Cumbria, the North East and the East and West Midlands, while the South covered London and the South East, the East and the South West

title: Wigan council 'listening' as warehouse plans dropped

input.lead: Wigan Council said it had listened and "struck the right balance" between supporting growth and creating jobs
input.summary: Wigan Council said it had listened and "struck the right balance" between supporting growth and creating jobs
input.evidence_text: Wigan council 'listening' as warehouse plans dropped - BBC News Image source, Joanna Allsop Image caption, Members of the Save Our Astley and Boothstown Greenbelt at a summer protest By Kevin Fitzpatrick North West Published 21 October 2026 A consultation is due to end on Wigan Council's plan for future development, with four sites potentially earmarked for warehouses being removed. It follows an outcry from residents over the construction of huge warehouses close to homes near Astley. The local authority said it had listened and "struck the right balance between supporting economic growth and job creation". Greenbelt campaigners and opposition councillors claimed they had forced the council to act. Councils must put together a local plan which identifies sites for housing and business development every decade or so and Wigan is in the process of updating its own. In the version under consultation, it has said four sites would not be taken forward. They include to the north of M6 junction 26, Moss Industrial Estate extension, Bridgewater West in Astley, and West of Winwick Lane in Lowton. The site being described as Bridgewater West is known locally as Higher Green and more than half a million sqaure feet of employment space was to have been built. Joanna Allsop from the Save Our Astley and Boothstown Greenbelt lives nearby and said; "It was just unbelievable that anyone could suggest that it could be anything other than Greenbelt." She said they are still concerned about its future, adding: "What we want is long-lasting protection. We want them to say that it is Greenbelt, not try to say that it's Greybelt." input.summary: This year marks 100 years since Wythenshawe Hall was donated to Manchester Corporation At the time, the city was in urgent need of more housing In 1920 an urban planner called Patrick Abercrombie identified Wythenshawe as the only undeveloped land suitable for building a housing
input.evidence_text: This year marks 100 years since Wythenshawe Hall was donated to Manchester Corporation At the time, the city was in urgent need of more housing In 1920 an urban planner called Patrick Abercrombie identified Wythenshawe as the only undeveloped land suitable for building a housing estate close to Manchester To turn his proposal into a reality, Ernest and Shena Simon bought Wythenshawe Hall from Robert Henry Grenville Tatton in 1926, which they donated to the city's corporation (now known as the council) The idea was that people could be rehoused away from industrial Manchester into what became known as the "Garden City" To celebrate 100 years, BBC North West Tonight has spoken to 100 people from the area about what Wythenshawe means to them

The property on Old Hall Lane, Broughton Park, is described by experts as a "strikingly glamourous" house Built in 1935 it is a rare example of the international Streamline Moderne style that evolved from Art Deco. It features curved corners, long horizontal "speed lines," and a sleek, machine-age look inspired by ocean liners, airplanes, and trains Other examples of the style include East Finchley Tube Station in London and the Coca Cola building in Los Angeles. The design is characterised by flat roofs, horizontal emphasis, curved corners and dramatic glazing From the outside, this house is distinguished by slim brown brick facades, a flat roof, an exposed white concrete base, and windows that span both curved and angled corners View 5 Images A curved stair tower dominates the back of the house, while the entrance front steps back in stages, with an original single-storey garage reflecting the growing importance of the car in home design between the First and Second World Wars

The property on Old Hall Lane, Broughton Park, is described by experts as a "strikingly glamourous" house Built in 1935 it is a rare example of the international Streamline Moderne style that evolved from Art Deco. It features curved corners, long horizontal "speed lines," and a sleek, machine-age look inspired by ocean liners, airplanes, and trains Other examples of the style include East Finchley Tube Station in London and the Coca Cola building in Los Angeles. The design is characterised by flat roofs, horizontal emphasis, curved corners and dramatic glazing From the outside, this house is distinguished by slim brown brick facades, a flat roof, an exposed white concrete base, and windows that span both curved and angled corners View 5 Images A curved stair tower dominates the back of the house, while the entrance front steps back in stages, with an original single-storey garage reflecting the growing importance of the car in home design between the First and Second World Wars

Figures for the financial year ending March 2026 show 5,617 betting shops in Great Britain, down 3.6% from a year earlier. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round
